title: Andy Burnham’s reshuffle: New jobs, old trade-offs
gist: Andy Burnham made John Healey — a defence secretary who resigned demanding more military spending — his chancellor and moved Ed Miliband from a rumoured Treasury posting to the Foreign Office, a shrewd manoeuvre that lets him wrap coming tax and borrowing rises in a national-defence appeal. The argument is that the politics will collide with arithmetic: the 'defence dividend' is a myth, defence spending is now capital- rather than labour-intensive, and Healey's 3 per cent of GDP by end-decade pledge makes his own fiscal dilemmas harder, with other public services and benefits the likely bill-payers.

themes.theme: The appointments and the political logic

insights.claim: Andy Burnham late-flipped Ed Miliband from the Treasury, where he was originally rumoured to be headed, to the Foreign Office, and appointed John Healey as chancellor — a man who spent six years focused entirely on international affairs in the defence brief before resigning in June.
insights.speaker: Tom Clark
insights.so_what: A chancellor with no recent economic preparation raises the probability of policy improvisation at the next fiscal event — an execution-risk premium for gilts and sterling.
insights.locator: No one would attribute Andy Burnham’s late flip

insights.claim: Escalating briefings against Ed Miliband from Labour factions that never forgave him for narrowly beating his brother David to the leadership in 2010 made handing him the Exchequer incompatible with Burnham's aim of party peace and reconciliation, and the Healey appointment fit that aim better.
insights.speaker: Tom Clark
insights.so_what: The chancellorship was allocated on factional-management grounds rather than economic competence — a signal about how future economic decisions will be arbitrated.

insights.claim: Handing Healey the keys to the Treasury he recently attacked — he had charged 'Treasury orthodoxy' with being a 'dead hand on dynamic government' when he quit demanding more defence cash — lets Burnham project a break with failed conventional economic wisdom and wrap coming rises in tax and perhaps borrowing in an appeal to national defence.
insights.speaker: Tom Clark
insights.so_what: Expect tax rises and possibly higher borrowing framed as rearmament rather than fiscal repair — the framing may reach voters normally hostile to Labour spending, so political resistance may be lower than markets assume.
insights.locator: There are additional layers of political cunning

insights.claim: Late expectations were that Ed Miliband could be pipped to the chancellorship by the more divisive Shabana Mahmood, making Healey the reconciliation-friendly outcome.
insights.speaker: Tom Clark
insights.so_what: The near-miss reveals how contested the economic direction is inside the new cabinet — leadership of fiscal policy is not settled.
insights.locator: This is especially so as it comes after late expectations

insights.claim: In his Downing Street address Burnham dispensed with the lists of missions and milestones Keir Starmer would drone through, instead issuing a single 'first instruction' to banish rough sleeping — a clear moral mission the whole Labour party can unite behind.
insights.speaker: Tom Clark
insights.so_what: The communications reset is real even where policy is not — a reminder that near-term polling improvement need not imply any change in fiscal or economic trajectory.
insights.locator: In a strong address at the door of 10 Downing Street

insights.claim: Clement Attlee's 1945 late swap — telling Hugh Dalton to pack a thin suit for Potsdam before installing him in the Treasury and taking Ernie Bevin to the conference instead — is the historical case that unexpected appointments can work out spectacularly, with Dalton financing the welfare state and Bevin driving Nato and the Council of Europe.
insights.speaker: Tom Clark
insights.so_what: A useful base rate: mismatched appointments occasionally produce transformative results, so dismissing Healey and Miliband on CV grounds alone is too quick — but the author's own view is that the conditions differ.
insights.quote: “Go home, pack, and put in a thin suit.”

insights.claim: The odds are stacked strongly against Burnham's appointments producing results comparable to Attlee's 1945 swap, even though the immediate politics look shrewd.
insights.speaker: Tom Clark
insights.so_what: The author's central call: political skill without a resolved economic plan, meaning the government's honeymoon should be treated as narrative rather than substance.
insights.locator: Never say never, but it seems to me

insights.claim: The Foreign Office job Bevin once held no longer exists: the UK is not one of the world's 'Big Three', sits outside Europe and is at the mercy of a capricious, aspiring authoritarian in Washington, so whatever diplomatic influence remains must largely be channelled by the prime minister himself at summits such as the G7.
insights.speaker: Tom Clark
insights.so_what: UK foreign-policy signal now comes from the PM's personal diplomacy, not the foreign secretary — read Burnham's summit behaviour, not FCDO statements, for direction on trade and EU re-engagement.
insights.quote: The Foreign Office job once done by Bevin no longer exists.
insights.locator: And yet all this crafty political strategy

insights.claim: Ed Miliband's realistic ceiling as foreign secretary is keeping climate diplomacy alive until the Trump era is over, rather than reshaping international affairs as Bevin did.
insights.speaker: Tom Clark
insights.so_what: A holding pattern on climate diplomacy implies no near-term UK-led acceleration in international climate finance or carbon policy — relevant for transition-exposed assets.
insights.locator: Miliband might hope to be an important voice

insights.claim: Ed Miliband is a former Chair of the Council of Economic Advisers with a Green New Deal agenda that the environmentalist Charles III would have quietly welcomed at the Treasury.
insights.speaker: Tom Clark
insights.so_what: The green-industrial economic agenda has been moved out of the Treasury — a negative signal for the scale of UK green investment programmes this parliament.
insights.locator: The environmentalist Charles III would have quietly smiled

themes.theme: The defence dividend is a myth

insights.claim: Despite hopeful talk of a 'defence dividend', the real payoff for the Exchequer and for living standards comes from peace, not from rearmament.
insights.speaker: Tom Clark
insights.so_what: Directly challenges the political case for defence-led growth — if correct, defence-spending increases should be modelled as a fiscal cost with crowding-out effects, not a growth stimulus.
insights.quote: Despite hopeful talk of a “defence dividend”, the real payoff for the Exchequer and for living standards comes from peace.
insights.locator: As for the Treasury, both Healey and Burnham

insights.claim: In the early postwar period the UK devoted roughly twice as much national income as West Germany to the armed services and many times what Japan spent, and the effect was not to propel the economy forward but to leave it lagging the pack.
insights.speaker: Tom Clark
insights.so_what: The historical comparison is the strongest empirical case against defence-led industrial strategy — a reason to be sceptical of UK defence primes' macro-growth narrative even while their order books grow.
insights.quote: The UK devoted roughly twice as much national income as the West Germans to the armed services in the early postwar period, and many times what the Japanese spent.
insights.locator: The UK devoted roughly twice as much national income

insights.claim: Modern defence expenditure is capital- rather than labour-intensive, so the promise of good jobs in weapons factories is weak, and resources consumed by defence cannot be consumed or more productively invested elsewhere in the economy.
insights.speaker: Tom Clark
insights.so_what: Defence spending increases should be expected to boost defence-sector margins and capital equipment demand without delivering broad regional employment gains — a narrower trade than the political rhetoric implies.
insights.quote: defence expenditure is capital- rather than labour-intensive these days
insights.locator: Yes, there are some jobs in weapons factories

insights.claim: If the Russian threat is grave enough the money will simply have to be found, but attempts to pretend it can be found in ways that leave the population better off will unravel into a message of sacrifice akin to the Second World War.
insights.speaker: Tom Clark
insights.so_what: Watch for the rhetorical shift from 'defence dividend' to 'sacrifice' — that transition is the political signal that real austerity or significant tax rises are imminent.
insights.locator: If the threat from Russia is grave enough

insights.claim: Other public services and the benefits that the hardest-pressed families rely on are the likely bill-payers for rearmament, following the pattern of Starmer slashing international aid to finance a first tranche of defence ambitions that he left office without funding in full.
insights.speaker: Tom Clark
insights.so_what: Anticipate welfare and departmental cuts as the funding source in coming fiscal events — a demand headwind for UK domestic consumer exposure.
insights.locator: Other public services, as well as the benefits

insights.claim: John Healey's full-throated insistence on a clear pathway to spending 3 per cent of national income on defence by the end of the decade will make the dilemmas facing him as incoming chancellor harder, not easier.
insights.speaker: Tom Clark
insights.so_what: A publicly committed 3 per cent of GDP defence path is a hard constraint on the fiscal envelope — the number against which all other spending decisions in this parliament should be scored.
insights.locator: In any case, Healey’s full-throated insistence

insights.claim: Whatever one thinks of Rachel Reeves's broader record, she was clear-eyed rather than hypnotised by 'Treasury orthodoxy' in grasping that a strong army and strong public finances cannot support each other.
insights.speaker: Tom Clark
insights.so_what: Rehabilitating Reeves's fiscal analysis implies the new government will rediscover the same constraints — do not price a genuine regime change in UK fiscal policy.
insights.quote: in grasping this reality she was clear-eyed, not simply hypnotised by “Treasury orthodoxy”.
insights.locator: And however one rates Rachel Reeves’s broader record

insights.claim: The incoming government will most likely find itself struggling, just as the last one did, with a painful trade-off between a strong army and strong public finances, unless Burnham and Healey settle on a much broader-based growth plan coupled with smart revenue-raisers.
insights.speaker: Tom Clark
insights.so_what: Base case is continuity of the Starmer-era fiscal bind under new branding — the trigger to revise that view would be a credible broad growth plan plus new revenue instruments.
insights.quote: A strong army and strong public finances may both be nice things to have, but that doesn’t mean they can support each other.
